result:
I want to write about attention, because it feels like the rarest thing I own.

Not the frantic, productivity kind of attention, where you stare harder at a screen until your eyes burn. I mean the slow kind. The kind you practice on a morning walk when you have nowhere urgent to be, when the light is still deciding what kind of day it wants to be, and you notice that the air smells faintly of wet pavement and coffee from someone else’s kitchen window. That kind of attention doesn’t accomplish anything. It just widens you a little.

I have been thinking lately that most of life happens in that widening. We tell stories about big events — graduations, moves, weddings, losses, new jobs, diagnoses — as if those are the plot. But the actual texture of being alive is not in the plot at all. It is in the thousand tiny repetitions: boiling water, waiting for toast, hearing the same bus brakes sigh at the same corner, folding the same sweater, saying goodnight in the same tired voice. We live almost entirely in the in-between, and then we are surprised when the in-between is what we miss most when it’s gone.

This morning I woke up a little before my alarm. The room was that blue-gray color that happens right before sunrise, when everything looks underwater. For a minute I didn’t reach for my phone. I just listened. There was a crow arguing somewhere on the roof, a truck backing up three streets over, the soft tick of the heater. My mind, as it always does, tried to sprint forward into the day’s list — emails, errands, things I said awkwardly yesterday and should have said differently. But I pulled it back, gently, the way you would pull a dog back from traffic. Stay here. It’s morning. Nothing has gone wrong yet.

There is a freedom in that moment before the world asks you to be someone. Before you are competent or funny or helpful or behind. You are just a warm body under a blanket, breathing. I think we underestimate how radical it is to allow ourselves to be unformed for a little while each day. No performance. No optimization. Just inhale, exhale, crow on the roof.

I made coffee, and I tried to actually taste it. This is harder than it sounds. To taste coffee you have to not also be reading the news and rehearsing a conversation and worrying about money. You have to let the heat fog your glasses a little. Mine was slightly too bitter today because I ground it too fine, but there was still that deep chocolate underneath, and the milk made it turn the color of river clay. I stood by the window and drank it while watching a neighbor try to coax her cat off a fence. She failed. The cat had that perfect, ancient disdain that cats have perfected over millennia. Eventually she laughed, gave up, and went back inside. Triumph for the cat. A small play in three acts, no tickets required.

That is what I mean by noticing. The world is constantly staging these tiny, free performances, and we walk right past them staring at rectangles.

I used to think noticing was passive, a thing you did when nothing important was happening. Now I think it is one of the most active things you can do. To pay attention is to make a choice about what is real. The economist models and the headlines and the feeds all insist that what is real is urgent, loud, large-scale. But when you pay close attention to your own life, you discover a different scale. What is real is your friend’s voice cracking a little when she talks about her dad. What is real is the way bread sounds when you slice it fresh and the crust shatters. What is real is the particular heaviness of your limbs after swimming, when your body feels both tired and clean.

I love libraries for this reason. They are buildings designed for slow attention. No one is in a hurry in a library, or if they are, they look faintly embarrassed about it. The light falls in dusty columns between the stacks. People whisper without being told to. You can browse with no goal and find a book on beekeeping next to a memoir about Antarctica next to a collection of letters from a lighthouse keeper in 1912. It reminds you that human curiosity is vast and weird and not at all algorithmic. No recommendation engine would suggest that you, a person who came in to return a novel, actually need a 300-page history of salt. But there it is. And maybe you do.

Trains are similar. On a train you are allowed to stare out the window without apology. Watching houses flicker by, laundry on lines, backyards full of trampolines and rusted grills and tomato plants in buckets — you get this gentle reminder that everyone is living an entire interior life as complicated as yours. That teenager with headphones is rehearsing how to break up with someone. That old man with the newspaper is worried about his wife’s test results. That toddler kicking the seat is experiencing the sheer existential joy of kicking a seat. We are all simultaneous. The world does not revolve around your worries, which is both humbling and an enormous relief.

Lately I have been trying to re-learn how to be bored. Real boredom, not the scroll-hole kind. The kind where you sit on a porch and watch clouds rearrange themselves and feel time stretch out, slightly uncomfortable at first, like a muscle you haven’t used. We have become so afraid of that discomfort that we fill every gap with input. Line at the grocery store? Phone. Elevator ride? Phone. Two minutes while pasta boils? Might as well check something. But those gaps used to be where thinking lived. Daydreaming. Remembering. Putting two distant ideas together and making a third. If we pave over every quiet moment, where does the mind go to play?

I don’t say this as someone who has figured it out. I lose hours to the feed like everyone else. I know the particular shame of looking up and realizing forty minutes have passed and I cannot name a single thing I saw, only that I feel vaguely anxious and behind. Attention is a practice, not a possession. You don’t achieve it once and keep it. You lose it and return, lose it and return, like meditation, like friendship, like keeping a plant alive.

Speaking of plants: mine are not thriving, exactly, but they are persistent. The pothos on my desk has one vine that reaches stubbornly toward the lamp, with leaves getting smaller and smaller the farther it goes, as if it is sending out scouts. I admire that. To keep reaching even when the light is insufficient. To make smaller leaves but still make them green. There is a lesson there I haven’t fully learned yet, but I feel it every time I water it and whisper, absurdly, “good job.”

Perhaps this is what getting older is: realizing that joy was never going to be in the grand arrival, but in becoming a person who can find the arrival inside the ordinary. Fresh sheets. The first bite of a peach in August when juice runs down your wrist. Laughing so hard with a friend that you can’t breathe and your stomach hurts and you both know you will reference this moment for years as shorthand for happiness. The smell of rain on hot concrete — petrichor, scientists call it, from the Greek for stone and the ichor of gods. Even the name is poetry. The blood of gods in the pavement.

I want to remember that grief and wonder often live in the same house. The same heart that aches when you hear a song your grandmother loved is the heart that can be cracked open by a sunset over a parking lot. Feeling deeply is not a bug. I used to try to be even-keeled, to avoid the lows by dampening the highs. It doesn’t work. You just get flat. Better to let the waves come. Better to stand in the rain of feeling and get soaked. You dry.

If I could give one piece of unsolicited advice — and I offer it mostly to myself — it would be this: keep a small notebook for beautiful sentences, overheard fragments, strange dreams, things that made you pause. Not for productivity. For proof. Proof that you were here and you noticed. “The moon looked like a thumbnail clipping last night.” “Old woman on bus told driver he drives like her late husband, ‘too fast and too kind.’” “My brother snorts when he laughs when he’s truly surprised.” These are not important data. They will not improve your resume. But years from now they will be a map back to who you were and what the world tasted like.

Because the world is always ending and beginning. Seasons turn whether we watch or not. People we love change, leave, return in different forms. Our bodies change. Our certainties change. Attention is the only way to hold any of it for even a second before it slips. Not to possess it, but to honor it. To say: I saw this. This mattered. You mattered. This morning light on the chipped mug mattered.

So today, if you can, take one slow look at something. Really look. At the veins in a leaf, at the way your partner’s eyes crinkle before they smile, at the steam curling off soup, at the city pigeons doing their iridescent-necked strut as if they own the sidewalk — which, honestly, they do. Let yourself be unproductive for five minutes. Let time pool around your feet instead of dragging you forward.

We have about, what, four thousand weeks if we are lucky? That sounds terrifying until you realize each week contains roughly ten thousand minutes of potential noticing. Ten thousand chances to taste, to hear, to feel the particular weight of being alive right now, in this body, on this spinning planet, under this same old sun that warmed dinosaurs and will warm whatever comes after us.

I find that oddly comforting. We are brief, but we are aware of our briefness, and that awareness can be luminous.

So here is my quiet manifesto for an ordinary day: drink the coffee while it’s hot. Look out the window longer than necessary. Text the friend you keep meaning to text. Walk a little slower past the garden with the overgrown rosemary. Let the cat stay on the fence. It’s not in the way. It is the way.
